_source.displaydescription:
The Nārāyaṇa Mandira (Temple) is located inside the Bāghabhairava Temple Complex (KIR0004) in Kirtipur. The door to its sanctum which is ornately designed and carved, rests on a stone pillar base (īlvahaṃ) and is flanked by a pair of stone lions. Generally, such a type of door architecture can be seen only in tiered temples. Thus, we can assume that the Nārāyaṇa Mandira too was originally a tiered-styled temple.

There are no historical sources to date the initial construction of this Temple. However, Ś. Śreṣṭha (VS 2057, 45), without refereeing to any sources, mentions that it was constructed by Hastikā (one of the nannies of King Raṇabahādura Śāha) in 1803 CE during the renovation of the Bāghabhairava Temple (KIR0004).

The Temple’s pinnacle is octagonal and is gilded. According to the elders of this area, the octagonal gilded pinnacle was established by a certain Jītavīra (who was supposedly a government employee), a resident of the Tuṃjhvaḥ Ṭola (Kirtipur) when he renovated the Temple in 1932 CE (VS 1988) by the order of Prime Minister Juddha Śamśera (r. 1 September 1932 - 29 November 1945). The inscription inscribed on the pinnacle records this information.

It was probably during this renovation the temple’s structure was changed from a tiered style to a domed style. Such a domed style temple architecture was popular during the time of Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā. From his time onwards, several damaged temples were reconstructed in the domed shape.

The present look of the Nārāyaṇa Mandira dates back to 1952 CE (VS 2009). Around the same time, a guṭhī was established to look after the Temple and conduct the daily rituals here ( Ś. Śṛeṣṭha, 1994, 87).

A statue of Śrīdharaviṣṇu standing on the samapāda posture is consecrated inside its sanctum. The statue has four arms: he is carrying a cakra (wheel) on his upper right hand and a gadā (mace) on his upper left hand. Similarly, a padma (lotus) is on his lower right hand and a śaṅkha (conch shell) is on his lower left hand.

The Śrīdharavisṇu statue is flanked by a Sarasvatī (left) and Lakṣmī (right) statue. These two female deities are believed to be Viṣṇu’s wives in the Kathmandu Valley from the medieval time (R. Vanta VS 2061, 19). Beside these, a statue of a donor couple in greeting posture (namaskāramudrā) is also erected inside the sanctum.

The descendants of Jītavīra who had renovated the Temple in 1932 CE used to clean the Temple premises, paint the Temple and perform its anniversary rituals. They had also endowed some plots of land for this purpose. However, this tradition came to an end sometime during the decade of 2000s CE (local knowledge, local resident, Maharjana, male, age 69).
